extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing, submitting, and evaluating 37 CFR 1.132 (Rule 132) declarations during patent prosecution, including timeliness, formal sufficiency, types of evidence, and how examiners must weigh and respond to declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Rule 132 declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: “When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under this section.” 37 CFR 1.132
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule gives applicants a way to provide evidence to overcome a ground of rejection or an objection. Note: affidavits are rare; the term 'declaration' used. All declarations not falling within specific rules are to be treated under this rule (MPEP 716). Office practice allows submission even where no rejection of record in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make a Rule 132 declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who has knowledge of the facts being asserted in the declaration may make a declaration under rule 132 (e.g., inventor, inventor’s co-worker, independent expert, or others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special qualifications are required. Declarant must have knowledge of facts asserted. MPEP 716.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule 132 declaration is considered timely if submitted prior to a final rejection; before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; after final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal (with required showing); with an RCE in certain utility/plant apps; or with a CPA in design apps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites: 37 CFR 1.116(e); 37 CFR 1.114 (RCE); 37 CFR 1.53(d) (CPA); MPEP 716.01(A). If submitted after a final rejection, applicant must provide a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the declaration (or other evidence) was necessary and not earlier presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission after notice of appeal but before appeal brief
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration under rule 132 may be admitted if received after appeal, but prior to filing an appeal brief, if the examiner determines that it overcomes all rejections under appeal and a showing of good and sufficient reasons why it was necessary and not earlier presented has been made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for examiner consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner must determine whether the declaration meets formal requirements (e.g., timeliness, signed, willful false statements clause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If formal requirements are met, the examiner must consider the declaration on the merits and explain in the next office action why it is sufficient or insufficient to overcome the traversed rejection(s). MPEP 716.01(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must acknowledge declaration in next office action
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines the declaration meets formal requirements, the examiner must consider it on the merits and explain in the next office action why it is sufficient or insufficient to overcome the traversed rejection(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sufficient, comments should be consistent with guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance (MPEP 1302.14): e.g., 'The declaration is sufficient to overcome the rejection...'. Where insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why: e.g., 'The declaration is insufficient to overcome the rejection because ...' General unsupported statements like 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with the scope of the claims' without explanation are insufficient. MPEP 716.01(A),(B); 37 CFR 1.68.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examiner signature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary examiner must sign an action that is responsive to a declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note explicitly required by MPEP 716.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner analysis questions for every declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a declaration, the examiner should ask: What is the specific purpose of the declaration? What does the declaration actually show and how does it attempt to show it? Does it show facts or opinions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analytic steps guide weighing and admissibility of the evidence in the declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish factual evidence from opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual evidence = a witnessed event, act, or occurrence (e.g., comparative test results, sales figures). Opinion = a statement expressing what the person thinks, believes, or infers (e.g., expert opinions on level of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types are given some weight, but opinions should not state the ultimate legal conclusion at issue. Conclusory statements without objective factual support (e.g., 'unexpected') are of limited evidentiary value. MPEP 716.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing evidence — preponderance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate determination of patentability must be based on consideration of the entire record based on a preponderance of the evidence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must make a 'fresh' consideration of the rejection when a rule 132 declaration is properly submitted. The rejection should be maintained where a preponderance of all the evidence indicates the claimed subject matter is unpatentable. 'Preponderance' means 'more likely than not.' MPEP 716.01(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be probative, evidence of secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, etc.) must be related to the claimed invention; examiner must determine whether there is a nexus between the invention as claimed and the entirety of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nexus denotes a legally and factually sufficient connection so the evidence should be considered in the nonobviousness determination. MPEP 716.01(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results — required showing
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut a prima facie case of obviousness, a declaration establishing unexpected results should present a comparison with the closest prior art, under substantially the same conditions except for the allegedly novel features, and show results that are actually unexpected and of statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the declaration should include: description of what was tested (must compare to closest prior art), description of test conditions (commensurate with claim scope), test results for both claimed invention and closest prior art, and analysis of results (MPEP 716.02(e)). Precisely what was done should be recited (steps, materials, results). Conclusory statements without showing actual test results for both the prior art and claimed invention are insufficient. The unexpected property must be due to claimed features (not unclaimed), and scope of showing must be commensurate with claim scope. Applicant is not required to compare to hypothetical combination products suggested by examiner's combination of references (MPEP 716.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurate-in-scope requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence (e.g., test conditions/results) must be commensurate in scope with the scope of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims reciting broad temperature ranges only allow evidence commensurate with the particular claim scope; evidence showing unexpected results only at temperatures higher than the broad claim may be commensurate only with a narrower dependent claim. See In re Clemens; MPEP discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success — nexus and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success is a secondary consideration for obviousness and requires a nexus between the claimed features and the commercial success; success must be due to the claimed features and not unclaimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaration should include at least: description of what was sold, features of the invention as claimed, description of the relevant market, information on advertising in the market, and other relevant information (MPEP 716.03). Sales results should include evidence of market share, total sales for competing products, differences between products, total sales for products embodying the invention, and pricing. Factors that undercut nexus include heavy promotion/advertising, brand name recognition, recent tech/consumer demand changes, consumption tied to applicant/assignee, and sales programs. Gross sales alone do not show commercial success absent market share evidence; inventor opinion alone is generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need — required showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-felt need is a secondary consideration for obviousness and a successful showing should include that (1) the need was persistent and recognized by those of ordinary skill, (2) the need was not satisfied by another before the effective filing date, and (3) the claimed invention in fact satisfies the long-felt need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should also show unsuccessful efforts by others to solve the problem; the mere passage of time is insufficient, and a prior art reference showing a solution negates long-felt need (MPEP 716.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief by experts constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted support: 'The skepticism of an expert, expressed before these Inventors proved him wrong, is entitled to fair evidentiary weight...' MPEP 716.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying by others — evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: More than the mere fact of copying is necessary to make that action significant because copying may be attributable to other factors (e.g., lack of concern for patent property, contempt for patentee's ability to enforce patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of copying is persuasive when an alleged infringer tried for a substantial length of time to design a similar product but failed, and then copied the claimed invention (MPEP 716.06). Copying evidence often arises in litigation rather than prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of references — required showing
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration asserting inoperability of a reference must show that the steps a person of ordinary skill would take to achieve the claimed results in the reference would not result in an operative invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is insufficient merely to show that the reference's reported results were not achieved. Failures by experimenters with no interest in succeeding should not be given great weight. If inoperability is asserted for features not relied upon by the examiner, the reference may still be effective as to other operative features. If a patent teaches the claimed invention, a patentee's statement that the disclosure was not intended to be used as applicant claims is immaterial. MPEP 716.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of applicant's disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence must support that a person of skill in the art would have been able to make and use the claimed invention based on the disclosure without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence used to supplement a specification that appears deficient must establish that the information needed to make the specification complete would have been known to those of ordinary skill in the art (MPEP 716.09).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing inherent disclosure in the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 132 declarations may be used to establish inherency where a claim is amended to recite a limitation not explicitly recited in the original application, or where a continuing application recites something not expressly mentioned in the parent case and benefit of the parent filing date is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner will evaluate whether the declaration presents facts that affirmatively establish the purported inherent feature is necessarily present; mere possibility is insufficient. MPEP 2112 and discussion in slides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting allegations of inherency in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations might rebut an examiner's position of inherency in prior art for anticipation (102) or obviousness (103); for product-by-process rejections, once examiner provides a rationale showing similarity, burden shifts to applicant to present evidence establishing an unobvious difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product claims may have properties presumed inherent in prior art; applicant must show property is not inherent when examiner provides rationale. See MPEP discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of common Rule 132 evidence to 35 U.S.C. 102 vs 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results, long-felt need, and commercial success are relevant to nonobviousness (103) but are not relevant to anticipation (102); lack of inherency in prior art is relevant to anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only lack of inherency in the prior art is relevant to anticipation rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 (Knowledge check C; MPEP guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Which kinds of declaration evidence should be given weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Factually based expert opinions on level of ordinary skill and data showing unexpected results should be given weight; conclusory statements that the claimed invention meets 35 U.S.C. 112 are not; multiple declarants offering opinion praise is opinion evidence but not an ultimate legal conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers: fact-based expert opinions and data showing unexpected results = True (give weight); conclusory legal statements = False (no weight); multiple opinion declarations praising merits = True (opinion evidence still admissible provided not legal conclusion). See Knowledge check D and MPEP 716.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney arguments do not substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney arguments cannot take the place of evidence; attorney statements are not evidence and must be supported by appropriate declarations when evidence is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of attorney statements that are not evidence and must be supported by declaration: statements regarding unexpected results, commercial success, solution of a long-felt need, inoperability of the prior art. MPEP 716.01(c)(II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner duties if declaration untimely or not entitled to consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines a declaration is not timely and not entitled to consideration, the examiner should explain the reasons in the next office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should state why untimely/not entitled; explanation should be more than general statements. (Knowledge check B and MPEP 716.01(A)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant procedural rights regarding declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant has the right to petition formal matters (e.g., denial of entry) and the right to appeal substantive matters to the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal sufficiency/propriety of 1.132 declarations are delegated to Technology Center Directors (MPEP 1002.02(c)). PTAB will consider the examiner's review of the declaration only as part of review of the appealed rejection.
